issue.title: Wrong variable names for column valued/table valued function parameters on Oracle

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

issue.body:
### Describe the bug

When using table-valued or column-valued functions in Oracle specifically, if the same function is used more than once, there is a collision in the parameter names being used. In the example below, `:ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3` is rendered for both calls, even though the parameters are different. All 6 parameters are correctly passed with unique names, but the query fails because it cannot bind the leftover ones.

### To Reproduce

```python
foobar_col = func.SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST("foo", "bar", "baz").column_valued("foobar")
snap_col = func.SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST("snap", "crackle", "pop").column_valued("snap")
numbers_col = func.SYS.ODCINUMBERLIST(1, 2, 3).column_valued("numbers")

my_query = select(foobar_col, snap_col)

print(my_query) # Parameter names are unique
print(my_query.compile(dialect=oracle.dialect())) # Parameter names are repeated!!

with oci_engine.begin() as conn:
    res = conn.execute(my_query)
    print(res.fetchall())
```


### Error

```
sqlalchemy.exc.DatabaseError: (cx_Oracle.DatabaseError) ORA-01036: illegal variable name/number
[SQL: SELECT COLUMN_VALUE foobar, COLUMN_VALUE snap 
FROM TABLE (SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST(:ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3)) foobar, TABLE (SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST(:ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3)) snap]
[parameters: {'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1': 'foo', 'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2': 'bar', 'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3': 'baz', 'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_4': 'snap', 'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_5': 'crackle', 'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_6': 'pop'}]
(Background on this error at: https://sqlalche.me/e/14/4xp6)
``` 

### Versions

- OS: Windows 10
- Python: 3.10.7
- SQLAlchemy: 1.4.44
- Database: Oracle 19c
- DBAPI : cx_oracle 8.3


### Additional context

Aditionnally, `COLUMN_VALUE` is always unqualified, meaning the above test query would fail even if the parameter numbering was correct. Below, the same example using two differently-named table-valued functions.

```py
>>> my_query2 = select(foobar_col, numbers_col)

>>> print(my_query2.compile(dialect=oracle.dialect()))
SELECT COLUMN_VALUE foobar, COLUMN_VALUE numbers 
FROM TABLE (SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST(:ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3)) foobar, TABLE (SYS.ODCINUMBERLIST(:ODCINUMBERLIST_1, :ODCINUMBERLIST_2, :ODCINUMBERLIST_3)) numbers


>>> with oci_engine.begin() as conn:
...     res = conn.execute(my_query2)
...     print(res.fetchall())

sqlalchemy.exc.DatabaseError: (cx_Oracle.DatabaseError) ORA-00918: column ambiguously defined
[SQL: SELECT COLUMN_VALUE foobar, COLUMN_VALUE numbers 
FROM TABLE (SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST(:ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3)) foobar, TABLE (SYS.ODCINUMBERLIST(:ODCINUMBERLIST_1, :ODCINUMBERLIST_2, :ODCINUMBERLIST_3)) numbers]
[parameters: {'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1': 'foo', 'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2': 'bar', 'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3': 'baz', 'ODCINUMBERLIST_1': 1, 'ODCINUMBERLIST_2': 2, 'ODCINUMBERLIST_3': 3}]
(Background on this error at: https://sqlalche.me/e/14/4xp6)
```

body:
**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**Oracle COLUMN_VALUE is a column name, not a keyword** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/4277

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **rel_1_4** branch:

**Oracle COLUMN_VALUE is a column name, not a keyword** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/4278

If I'm not wrong, the proposed fix causes `column_valued("foo")` to behave differently between Postgres and Oracle? It's unclear to me whether the first parameter for that method is meant to be a shortcut for the resulting column label or as an alias for the implicitly joined table. [The documentation examples](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/14/tutorial/data_select.html#column-valued-functions-table-valued-function-as-a-scalar-column) for Postgres show the latter, but also has the former as a side-effect due to how Postgres does things.

In Postgres, for example...
```sql
SELECT x, y
FROM json_array_elements('["one", "two"]') AS x, json_array_elements('["three", "four"]') AS y
```

...seems to be a shortcut for...
```sql
SELECT x.value as x, y.value as y
FROM json_array_elements('["one", "two"]') AS x, json_array_elements('["three", "four"]') AS y
```

Oracle currently uses the `name` parameter for both the column label and the table alias (seemingly by mistake) and the patch removes the former behavior, making all such columns inherit the "COLUMN_VALUE" label instead and requiring the label to be set by hand.

**EDIT:** Having `column_valued` set the column label seems more intuitive, since [it would mirror](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/14/tutorial/data_select.html#table-valued-functions) how `table_valued("col1", "col2")` works (parameters are for the column names, and the table still counted as anonymous until given an alias). TableValuedColumn also never exposes the corresponding table object, and it doesn't seem like the joining behavior can be controlled (on purpose, I would imagine, given the kind of function involved), so I'm not certain what the benefit of setting the name of that implicit table element would be.

How strange.



> In Postgres, for example...
> 
> ```sql
> SELECT x, y
> FROM json_array_elements('["one", "two"]') AS x, json_array_elements('["three", "four"]') AS y
> ```
> 
> ...seems to be a shortcut for...
> 
> ```sql
> SELECT x.value as x, y.value as y
> FROM json_array_elements('["one", "two"]') AS x, json_array_elements('["three", "four"]') AS y
> ```

this seems to be function dependent on postgres. For example there is no value in `generate_series`

```sql
SELECT x
FROM pg_catalog.generate_series(1, 5) x
```

> If I'm not wrong, the proposed fix causes `column_valued("foo")` to behave differently between Postgres and Oracle? It's unclear to me whether the first parameter for that method is meant to be a shortcut for the resulting column label or as an alias for the implicitly joined table. 

it's the name for the implicitly created table.   

> In Postgres, for example...
> 
> ```sql
> SELECT x, y
> FROM json_array_elements('["one", "two"]') AS x, json_array_elements('["three", "four"]') AS y
> ```
> 
> ...seems to be a shortcut for...
> 
> ```sql
> SELECT x.value as x, y.value as y
> FROM json_array_elements('["one", "two"]') AS x, json_array_elements('["three", "four"]') AS y
> ```

does not seem too different from "select x.COLUMN_VALUE, y.COLUMN_VALUE", however for the label thing, if you want the column expression to have a specific name, label() can be used for that:   `fn.column_value('x').label('x')`


> 
> Oracle currently uses the `name` parameter for both the column label and the table alias (seemingly by mistake) and the patch removes the former behavior, making all such columns inherit the "COLUMN_VALUE" label instead and requiring the label to be set by hand.

oh, because what I thought was the name of the table was actually the label name in practice, which was completely inadvertent.    I think this is a very new feature that hasn't seen much real world testing so I think it's more important to make the behavior what was intended, to the degree that someone was selecting a single-column result (since that's all that worked, unless they were combining with other table columns?  is that what you have in existing code?) and then looking for the value by name I think that is probably not a likely use case.

 
> **EDIT:** Having `column_valued` set the column label seems more intuitive, since [it would mirror](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/14/tutorial/data_select.html#table-valued-functions) how `table_valued("col1", "col2")` works (parameters are for the column names, and the table still counted as anonymous until given an alias). 

we don't implicltly create identifiable label names where no label is normally implied anywhere else, except for this one construct where it was completely by accident.   I'd rather push through with how it was intended to work, and a specific label name as always is available by calling ".label()" (which also probably didnt work with the previously broken syntax).

otherwise if this is decided that it's a major incompatible change, I would rather push the feature as intended to 2.0 without implementing a non-intended API in 1.4, that is, it stays broken (which I dont think is what we should do).


> TableValuedColumn also never exposes the corresponding table object, and it doesn't seem like the joining behavior can be controlled (on purpose, I would imagine, given the kind of function involved), so I'm not certain what the benefit of setting the name of that implicit table element would be.

we are going for someone being able to control what the SQL looks like; you can omit that name and an anonymized name will be chosen.   similarly with the column expression, if someone doesn't set .label(), we dont want to render any label other than an anonymized one.

yeah the existing way is simply broken:

```py
my_query = select(foobar_col.label('q'))
```

```
(cx_Oracle.DatabaseError) ORA-00923: FROM keyword not found where expected
[SQL: SELECT COLUMN_VALUE foobar AS q 
FROM TABLE (SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST(:ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3)) foobar]

```

the column_value thing in Oracle was like a small "bonus" that I implemented because it "seemed to work", after the vast majority of the effort was for PostgreSQL which is where people look for this thing.  I'd really like to just fix the bug and not try to contort around how it accidentally "worked" under very specific constraints.

it looks like SQLAlchemy's column targeting is assigning the table name in the column description in any case.  this is also a little mysterious to me, but suggests the change won't really be backwards incompatible with that case anyway:

```py
my_query = select(foobar_col)

e = create_engine("oracle+cx_oracle://scott:tiger@oracle18c/xe", echo="debug")

with e.begin() as conn:
    res = conn.execute(my_query)
    for row in res:
        # works.  row._mapping['COLUMN_VALUE'] does not
        print(row._mapping['foobar'])


```

this despite the output showing COLUMN_VALUE as what cursor.description gave us:

```
SELECT foobar.COLUMN_VALUE 
FROM TABLE (SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST(:ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3)) foobar
2022-12-07 18:04:18,223 INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00020s] {'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1': 'foo', 'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2': 'bar', 'ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3': 'baz'}
2022-12-07 18:04:18,225 DEBUG sqlalchemy.engine.Engine Col ('COLUMN_VALUE',)
2022-12-07 18:04:18,226 DEBUG sqlalchemy.engine.Engine Row ('foo',)

```

that is, this is fine:

```py

with e.begin() as conn:
    for q in [
        select(foobar_col, snap_col),
        select(foobar_col.label('foobar'), snap_col.label('snap'))
    ]:

        res = conn.execute(q)
        for row in res:
            print(row._mapping['foobar'], row._mapping['snap'])


```

> this seems to be function dependent on postgres. For example there is no value in `generate_series`
> 
> ```sql
> SELECT x
> FROM pg_catalog.generate_series(1, 5) x
> ```

Hm, yeah, that's weird, `SELECT * FROM generate_series(1, 5)` does seem to act as if the function had been called as `SELECT generate_series(1, 5)`, unlike with `json_array_elements`. That's kind of quirky, but now that I'm looking at it, I would imagine this is actually meant to mirror `json_each`, which returns key and value columns. Nevermind that, then.



> I think it's more important to make the behavior what was intended, to the degree that someone was selecting a single-column result (since that's all that worked, unless they were combining with other table columns? is that what you have in existing code?) and then looking for the value by name I think that is probably not a likely use case.

I'm currently using these functions to do something like this:

```py

foobar_col = func.SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST("foo", "bar", "baz").column_valued("foobar")
numbers_col = func.SYS.ODCINUMBERLIST(1, 2, 3).column_valued("numbers")

foobar_subq = select(column("rownum").label("row_number"), foobar_col ).subquery()
numbers_subq = select(column("rownum").label("row_number"), numbers_col ).subquery()

# This would curently work
values_construct = select(foobar_subq.c.foobar, numbers_subq.c.numbers).select_from(
	foobar_subq.join(numbers_subq, foobar_subq.c.row_number == numbers_subq.c.row_number)
)

print(values_construct.compile(dialect=oracle.dialect()))
```

```sql
SELECT anon_1.foobar, anon_2.numbers 
FROM (SELECT rownum AS row_number, COLUMN_VALUE foobar 
FROM TABLE (SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST(:ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3)) foobar) anon_1 JOIN (SELECT rownum AS row_number, COLUMN_VALUE numbers 
FROM TABLE (SYS.ODCINUMBERLIST(:ODCINUMBERLIST_1, :ODCINUMBERLIST_2, :ODCINUMBERLIST_3)) numbers) anon_2 ON anon_1.row_number = anon_2.row_number
```

...with the intent of using this to emulate `values()` (so I can join on a dynamically defined table) on Oracle. The new branch wouldn't work unless I add `.label("foobar")` after `column_valued("foobar")` (which doesn't work on the current version of SQLA), and replacing `foobar_subq.c.foobar` in the final ``select()`` by `foobar_col` (which usually works well in-lieu of using column names, where those would be ambiguous) results in the `table()` clause being implicitly cross-joined on the outer query. Using `label()` on `column_valued` tables right now results in invalid SQL, as you pointed out, so wouldn't that be a breaking change in that regard?

(Not that I'm using this in production yet, because of the bound parameter issue, but it's surprising behavior to me, besides the hypothetical possibility of breaking existing and working code)



> we are going for someone being able to control what the SQL looks like; you can omit that name and an anonymized name will be chosen. similarly with the column expression, if someone doesn't set .label(), we dont want to render any label other than an anonymized one.

I'm not seeing any anonymized (column) labels being rendered in the logs you've posted so far from the bugfixed branch.

> Using label() on column_valued tables right now results in invalid SQL, as you pointed out, so wouldn't that be a breaking change in that regard?

well the previous behavior was a bug. I think it's fair to make breaking changes to fix bugs.

On the main branch this now renders as 
```sql
SELECT anon_1.foobar, anon_2.numbers
FROM (SELECT rownum AS row_number, foobar.COLUMN_VALUE
FROM TABLE (SYS.ODCIVARCHAR2LIST(:ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_1, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_2, :ODCIVARCHAR2LIST_3)) foobar) anon_1 JOIN (SELECT rownum AS row_number, numbers.COLUMN_VALUE
FROM TABLE (SYS.ODCINUMBERLIST(:ODCINUMBERLIST_1, :ODCINUMBERLIST_2, :ODCINUMBERLIST_3)) numbers) anon_2 ON anon_1.row_number = anon_2.row_number
```
that I haven't run, but I'm guessing it's not working, since oracle can't find `anon_1.foobar` or `anon_2.numbers`.
I think in other cases we assign anon labels to the subqery columns, and render the external one as `anon_1.anon_col`

For example this gives
```py
foobar_subq = (
    select(column("rownum").label("row_number"), func.max(column("x")))
    .select_from(table("a"))
    .subquery()
)
numbers_subq = (
    select(column("rownum").label("row_number"), func.min(column("y")))
    .select_from(table("a"))
    .subquery()
)

values_construct = select(foobar_subq.c.max, numbers_subq.c.min).select_from(
    foobar_subq.join(
        numbers_subq, foobar_subq.c.row_number == numbers_subq.c.row_number
    )
)

print(values_construct.compile(dialect=oracle.dialect()))

```
```sql
SELECT anon_1.max_1, anon_2.min_1
FROM (SELECT rownum AS row_number, max(x) AS max_1
FROM a) anon_1 JOIN (SELECT rownum AS row_number, min(y) AS min_1
FROM a) anon_2 ON anon_1.row_number = anon_2.row_number
```
